question.problem: Given the curve $r(t)=⟨1-{t}^{2},3t+4⟩,$ find the point at which the tangent to the curve is perpendicular to the vector $⟨1,1⟩.$
question.worked_solution:
First, we calculate the derivative of $r(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1-{t}^{2}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3t+4)⟩ \\  & =⟨-2t,3⟩\end{aligned}
$$

The vectors $⟨1,1⟩$ and ${r}^{′}(t)$ are perpendicular for some value of the parameter $t$ if and only if $⟨1,1⟩\cdot {r}^{′}(t)=0.$ So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨1,1⟩\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =0 \\ ⟨1,1⟩\cdot ⟨-2t,3⟩ & =0 \\ 1(-2t)+1(3) & =0 \\ -2t+3 & =0 \\ t & =\frac{3}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the only solution is $t=\frac{3}{2}.$

Finally, since

$$
\begin{aligned}r(\frac{3}{2}) & =⟨1-{(\frac{3}{2})}^{2},3(\frac{3}{2})+4⟩ \\  & =⟨1-\frac{9}{4},\frac{9}{2}+4⟩ \\  & =⟨-\frac{5}{4},\frac{17}{2}⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

we conclude that $⟨1,1⟩$ and ${r}^{′}(t)$ are perpendicular at the point $(-\frac{5}{4},\frac{17}{2}).$
